analysis.one_liner: Ends qualified immunity for police officers and makes it easier to criminally charge officers whose conduct kills someone.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House on January 30, 2026 with no cosponsors and has sat in the Judiciary Committee since referral, with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill does two things. First, it strips away 'qualified immunity' — the court-created shield that lets police officers avoid civil lawsuits unless the victim can point to a past court case where nearly identical conduct was ruled illegal. Second, it makes it easier to bring federal criminal charges when police misconduct kills someone, by lowering the required mental state from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly' and by counting any act that was a substantial factor in the death. It also removes the death penalty as a possible punishment in those federal cases. The bill was introduced by a single representative with no cosponsors and has not moved in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by police misconduct and their families, who today often cannot win a civil lawsuit or secure a criminal conviction because of the intent standard and the immunity doctrine. Communities affected by police violence gain a practical path to hold officers accountable in civil court.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds language to 42 U.S.C. 1983 making it impossible for local and federal law enforcement officers to defend a civil rights lawsuit by claiming good faith, a reasonable belief their conduct was lawful, or that the violated right was not 'clearly established' at the time. Today, that 'clearly established' rule is the main reason many legitimate civil suits against officers are dismissed before a jury ever hears them.

The bill lowers the mental state required for a federal criminal charge under 18 U.S.C. 242 from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly' when the deprivation of rights results in death, and adds a rule that an act counts as resulting in death if it was a substantial factor contributing to the death. The current 'willfully' standard is one of the highest intent bars in federal criminal law, and it is a major reason officers are rarely convicted when someone dies in police custody or during an arrest.
The bill removes the death penalty as a sentencing option in these federal civil rights cases, taking the most severe punishment off the table even as it lowers the bar for prosecution.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers, who lose the immunity defense in civil suits and face easier criminal prosecution in death cases; and local governments and their insurers, which typically indemnify officers and would absorb more settlement and litigation costs. Police departments could also face higher liability costs and changed training and conduct incentives.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the 'clearly established' requirement and the good-faith defense entirely, so officers could face civil suits for conduct they had no reasonable way to know was illegal. Supporters of the current doctrine argue this exposes officers to personal financial and career risk for split-second decisions, and that fear of litigation can chill proactive policing in high-crime neighborhoods.

Lowering the criminal intent standard to 'recklessly' makes it possible to convict an officer for a death based on a lower threshold of fault than the current 'willfully' standard, which was written to protect officers acting under color of law. Critics argue that split-second use-of-force decisions are poorly judged in hindsight and that the change risks criminalizing honest mistakes.

Because local governments almost always indemnify officers for civil judgments, the practical cost of expanded civil liability may fall on taxpayers through settlements and insurance rather than on the individual officers being sued.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses two real barriers that routinely block accountability: qualified immunity gets cases dismissed before trial, and the 'willfully' standard makes criminal convictions nearly impossible even in widely documented deaths. The trade-off is genuine — ending all good-faith protections could expose officers to suits over conduct that was arguably reasonable at the time, and the recklessly standard would make prosecution easier in ambiguous cases. The death-penalty repeal partially offsets the harsher criminal standard. Whether the balance is right depends on how much weight one gives to officer risk versus the current near-total difficulty of holding officers accountable in court.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by one representative, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and has not been taken up since — with zero cosponsors two weeks in, it looks headed for the same committee shelf where similar police-accountability bills have stalled for years.

narrative.text: Rep. Julie Johnson of Texas introduced the bill on January 30, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill has zero cosponsors as of the latest cosponsor count.
The only action after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the House on February 4, 2026; no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled.

The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, which contained a qualified-immunity provision and from which this bill borrows its officer definition, passed the House in a prior Congress but stalled in the Senate, a precedent for how police-accountability legislation has fared even with more support than this bill has.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and the unions that defend the qualified-immunity doctrine are better off for now, because the bill sits untouched in committee with no cosponsors and no path to a vote. People harmed by police misconduct are no worse off than before, but they gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police unions and officers keep the status quo

for.name: Rep. Julie Johnson
for.role: U.S. Representative, TX-32; sole sponsor of the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; recruited no cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the bill is sponsored by one Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so no party position has been tested.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill removes qualified immunity — the doctrine that shields officers from most civil suits over misconduct — and lowers the criminal intent standard in death cases. Unions have historically been the primary defenders of the doctrine, arguing officers need protection for split-second decisions.

industries.industry: Municipal governments and their liability insurers
industries.note: Cities typically pay civil judgments against officers through indemnification and insurance, so expanded civil liability would raise their settlement and premium costs. Some of that cost may ultimately come from taxpayers, and insurers could raise premiums in high-litigation jurisdictions.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors nearly two weeks after introduction, no hearing or markup scheduled, and a Judiciary Committee majority that has not taken up similar police-accountability legislation in recent years, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee and expires at the end of the Congress without a vote. A surge of cosponsors or public attention could change that, but nothing in the record suggests it is coming.
